questions.q: What is the main difference between 'top-down' and 'bottom-up' ways of making nanostructures?
options: Top-down carves a larger piece into shape; bottom-up lets atoms come together and grow into the structure
Top-down grows crystals from atoms; bottom-up cuts a large crystal into small pieces
Top-down works only for metals; bottom-up works only for semiconductors
Top-down is done at low temperature; bottom-up is done at high temperature
questions.explain: Top-down carves, like a sculptor, and puts structures exactly where they were drawn. Bottom-up grows them, like a crystal, making near-perfect crystals by the billion. The best devices often combine the two.

questions.q: Electron-beam lithography can write features below 10 nm. Why are chips still made by photolithography instead?
options: Photolithography prints a whole pattern at once through a mask, while an electron beam writes one point at a time
Electron beams damage silicon so badly that no transistor made with them works
Photolithography can print much smaller features than an electron beam
Electron beams can only be used on glass, not on silicon wafers
questions.explain: An electron beam writes like a very fine pen, one point at a time: good for research and one-off devices. Photolithography prints the whole pattern at once through a mask, which is how chips are made in billions.

questions.q: Why do quantum dots carved by etching glow poorly?
options: The carved walls are rough and damaged, and in a small dot most atoms are near them, so electrons are trapped before they can give out light
Etching removes the electrons from the dot along with the material, so there are too few left to give out light
Etched dots are always too large to show quantum effects
The resist stays on top of the dot and blocks the light
questions.explain: Carved walls are rough at the atomic scale. In a 20 nm dot most atoms are near them, so the damage spoils the light emission.

questions.q: Why is molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) used to grow quantum wells?
options: It builds the crystal about one layer of atoms at a time, and shutters give boundaries sharp to a single layer
It carves the wells out of a thick crystal with a beam of molecules
It grows crystals in a liquid at room temperature, so it is very cheap
It can grow hundreds of wafers at once, faster than any other method
questions.explain: MBE uses beams of atoms in an extremely high vacuum to build the crystal about one atomic layer per second, with shutters giving layer-sharp boundaries. MOCVD is faster and handles many wafers: almost every LED and laser diode is grown that way.

questions.q: The picture shows InAs being grown on GaAs. Why do islands (quantum dots) form after about 1.7 layers of atoms?
questions.alt: Four stages: 1 layer flat; at 1.7 layers a complete wetting layer; at 2.2 layers islands appear; at 3 layers dense dots
options: InAs atoms are spaced about 7% further apart than GaAs, so the squeezed film relieves its strain by bunching into islands
The GaAs surface is dirty, so the InAs sticks only to the dirty spots
A pattern is drawn on the surface first, and the islands then grow only where that pattern was drawn
The InAs film melts once it reaches that thickness and forms droplets that later freeze into islands
questions.explain: InAs is squeezed to fit the GaAs underneath, like a carpet too big for its room. After about 1.7 layers it bunches up into islands: self-assembled dots. No pattern is drawn and nothing is removed.

questions.q: True or false: Stranski–Krastanov growth of self-assembled dots is a hybrid method that combines a drawn pattern with growth.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. It is purely bottom-up: no pattern is drawn and nothing is removed; the dots assemble themselves. (The original handout's claim that it is a hybrid, and that islands appear after ten layers, are both wrong.)

questions.q: The picture shows dots made by hot injection. Why do the dots in one batch come out nearly the same size?
questions.alt: A flask of hot liquid with a syringe injecting a solution, and a row of vials of dots taken out at times from 10 s to 1 h
options: All the seeds are born in one quick burst, then grow together for the same time
The liquid is filtered at the end to throw away all the dots of the wrong size
Each dot is grown separately in its own tiny container
The dots are carved to size with a beam of electrons after they have grown
questions.explain: Injection at about 300 °C makes a burst of seed crystals in a fraction of a second. At a slightly lower temperature the seeds grow but no new ones form, so they stay nearly the same size, often within 5%.

questions.q: A television screen needs billions of dots of exactly the right colour, but their positions do not matter. Which way of making the dots suits it best?
options: Chemistry in a hot flask (colloidal dots)
Electron-beam lithography and etching
Self-assembled growth by molecular-beam epitaxy
Focused ion beam milling, one dot at a time
questions.explain: The application chooses the method. A television needs billions of dots of the right colour, anywhere: chemistry. A quantum computer needs a few dots in exactly the right places: lithography and voltages. A laser needs perfect crystals in a thin layer: epitaxy.

questions.q: The picture shows a finished quantum dot. What does the ZnS shell around the core do?
questions.alt: A round core of CdSe or InP surrounded by a ZnS shell, with long ligand chains sticking out like hairs
options: It keeps the electron and hole inside the core, away from surface traps, so the dot glows far more brightly
It absorbs ultraviolet light from outside, so that the core is not damaged by sunlight
It changes the colour of the dot, shifting the light it gives out from green to red
It lets the dot pass electrons to its neighbours, so that a film of dots conducts
questions.explain: Bare surfaces trap electrons and stop the glow. A shell such as ZnS keeps the electron and hole in the core, raising the light given out from a few per cent to over 90%. The ligands, like hairs, keep the dots apart and let them be mixed into inks.

questions.q: Which method is used most today to grow carbon nanotubes, and why?
options: Chemical vapour deposition: carbon-rich gas over metal particles, which scales up and can grow tubes on wafers
Arc discharge: a big spark between carbon rods, which gives tubes already sorted by type
Laser ablation: a laser vaporising carbon, which is the cheapest method
Lithography: carving the tubes from a block of graphite
questions.explain: Arc discharge (1991) and laser ablation came first, but chemical vapour deposition, with a carbon-rich gas over metal particles at 600–1000 °C, scales up and grows tubes directly on wafers.
